units.title: Foundation of Functions
units.intro: Independent x, dependent y. Function: each x → one y. Solve ax+b=c by inverse ops both sides. Inequality: flip the sign when you multiply/divide by a negative. Direct: y=kx. Inverse: y=k/x. |x|=a means x=a or x=−a (a≥0).

cards.title: 2.1.1 Dependent and independent quantities
body: Abrehet sells eggs in Keren at 3 Nakfa each. Her **income depends on** the number of eggs she sells: 10 eggs → 30 Nakfa, 18 eggs → 54 Nakfa.
- The quantity we choose or control (number of eggs) is the **independent quantity**.
- The quantity that changes **because of** it (income) is the **dependent quantity**.
Test: say "**___ depends on ___**". The first blank is dependent, the second is independent. "Income depends on eggs sold" — not "eggs depend on income".
In a **function**, each value of the independent quantity gives **exactly one** value of the dependent quantity.

cards.title: Domain and range
body: The **domain** is the set of all possible values of the independent quantity; the **range** is the set of all values the dependent quantity can take.
Kelifa's exam has 30 questions, 2 marks each. He can get 0, 1, 2, …, 30 questions right, so
$$\text{Domain} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots, 30\}, \quad \text{Range} = \{0, 2, 4, \dots, 60\}$$
Always think about what is **possible** in the real situation: you cannot answer $2.5$ questions or $-1$ questions.

cards.title: A function pairs each input with one output
body: Left: each number of correct answers goes to exactly one score, score $= 2 \times$ (correct answers) — a function. Right: the input 4 has two outputs, 2 and $-2$ — not a function.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Tables and graphs
body: A function can be shown as a **table of values**, which is a list of **ordered pairs** (input, output). Plot them with the **independent quantity on the horizontal ($x$) axis** and the dependent quantity on the vertical ($y$) axis.
The first number of a pair is always the input: $(1, 2)$ means "1 correct answer gives 2 marks"; $(2, 1)$ would mean something different.

cards.title: Fig. 2.2: score against correct answers (discrete)
body: The points are **separate dots** — you cannot get 2.5 answers right, so nothing lies between them. This is a **discrete graph**.

cards.title: Discrete or continuous?
head: Discrete graph
Continuous graph
rows: only separate values (counts: people, eggs, pages)
every real number in an interval (time, length, mass)
score vs correct answers; entrance money vs people
distance vs time; area vs side length
"Can the input be a fraction?" → No
"Can the input be a fraction?" → Yes
body: Rule of thumb: if you **count** the input it is discrete; if you **measure** it, it is continuous.

cards.title: Same table, two graphs (Example 2.2)
body: Walking 25 km at 5 km/h: remaining distance $d = 25 - 5t$. Plotting only whole hours gives dots; allowing every moment $t$ (0.1 h, 3.5 h, …) fills the gaps with a straight segment.

cards.title: 2.1.3 Describing a function with an equation
body: An equation states the rule in one line. Let $x$ = independent variable and $y$ = dependent variable.
- Kelifa: $y = 2x$. Abrehet: $y = 3x$.
- Water tank with 10 litres leaking 0.2 litre per hour: $y = 10 - 0.2x$ (empty when $x = 50$ hours).
- From a table, look at how $y$ changes when $x$ goes up by 1. If it always changes by the same amount $m$, the rule is $y = mx + c$, where $c$ is the value of $y$ when $x = 0$.

Continuous graphs represent variables that can take on any real value (like fractions of a second or decimal distances), while discrete graphs represent countable, distinct items.

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: 2.2.1 Solving equations: keep the balance
body: Two equations with the same solution set are **equivalent**: $2x + 3 = 13$ and $2x = 10$ both have solution set $\{5\}$. Solving means changing the equation, step by step, into simpler equivalent equations until it reads $x = $ number.
Think of a balance scale: whatever you do to one pan you must do to the other.

steps.text: Each box weighs $x$ balls. The scale shows $2x + 3 = 9$.
Remove 3 balls from **both** pans (subtract 3): the scale stays level.
Now $2x = 6$. Split both pans into two equal halves (divide by 2).

cards.title: Moves that keep an equation equivalent
body: 1. Add the same number to both sides. 2. Subtract the same number from both sides.
3. Multiply both sides by the same **non-zero** number. 4. Divide both sides by the same **non-zero** number.
5. Replace an expression by an equal one (e.g. expand brackets). 6. Swap the two sides.

steps.text: Divide both sides by 3: $8 = y$, so $y = 8$.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Variables on both sides
body: Recipe: (1) expand brackets; (2) move all $x$-terms to one side and numbers to the other by adding/subtracting; (3) divide by the coefficient of $x$; (4) check in the **original** equation.
Tip: move the $x$-terms to the side with the **bigger** coefficient to avoid negative coefficients.

- **Decimals:** multiply every term by 10, 100, … to make all coefficients whole numbers.
Example 2.6: $0.2x + 2 = 2.6$. Multiply by 10: $2x + 20 = 26$, so $2x = 6$ and $x = 3$.

steps.text: LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. Multiply every term by 12: $3(x - 2) - 2(x + 5) = -24$.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Linear inequalities: one extra rule
body: Solve an inequality exactly like an equation, with **one** extra rule:
**When you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign** ($<$ becomes $>$, $\le$ becomes $\ge$). Swapping the two sides also reverses it ($5 > x$ means $x < 5$).
Why? $2 < 3$ is true, but multiplying by $-1$ gives $-2$ and $-3$, and $-2 > -3$.
An inequality usually has **infinitely many** solutions, so we write a set $\{x : x \ge 1\}$ and draw it on a number line: closed dot for $\le, \ge$; open dot for $<, >$.

cards.title: Solving equations and inequalities — the rules
body: **Linear equation:** do the same operation to both sides until x is alone. Example: 5x − 7 = 2x + 8 → 3x = 15 → x = 5. Check: 5(5) − 7 = 18 = 2(5) + 8 ✔.
**Equations with fractions:** multiply every term by the LCD first. (x/3) + (x/4) = 7 → 4x + 3x = 84 → x = 12.
**Absolute value:** |x − 2| = 5 means x − 2 = 5 or x − 2 = −5, so x = 7 or x = −3. (|x| = −1 has no solution.)

**Linear inequality:** same steps as an equation, BUT when you multiply or divide by a negative number, reverse the sign. −3x < 12 → x > −4. Show the answer on a number line (open circle for < or >, filled circle for ≤ or ≥) or in interval notation, e.g. (−4, ∞).

cards.title: 2.3.1 Direct variation
body: $y$ **varies directly** with $x$ if $y = kx$ for a constant $k \ne 0$, i.e. the **ratio** $\frac{y}{x} = k$ never changes. $k$ is the **constant of proportionality**.
Signs: when $x$ doubles, $y$ doubles; when $x$ is halved, $y$ is halved. The graph is a straight line **through the origin**.
Examples: distance and time at a fixed speed ($d = 5t$); income and eggs sold ($I = 3n$); profit and inventory.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Inverse variation
body: $y$ **varies inversely** as $x$ if $xy = k$, i.e. $y = \frac{k}{x}$ with $k \ne 0$. The **product** never changes.
Signs: when $x$ doubles, $y$ is halved. The graph is a curve that falls and never touches the axes.
Example: Nejat rides 10 km to school. Speed $\times$ time $= 10$: at 10 km/h she needs 1 h, at 20 km/h only 0.5 h.

cards.title: Direct and inverse variation compared
head: Direct
Inverse
body: Method for every variation problem: (1) write the type of equation, (2) use the given pair to find $k$, (3) use $k$ with the new value.

cards.title: Direct vs inverse: "divide or multiply"
body: **Direct:** y ÷ x stays the same (y = kx) — both go up together.
**Inverse:** y × x stays the same (y = k/x) — one up, the other down.

cards.title: 2.4.1 Absolute value = distance from 0
body: The **absolute value** $|x|$ is the distance of $x$ from 0 on the number line. A distance is never negative, so $|x| \ge 0$ always.
$$|x| = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0 \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}$$
So $|6| = 6$ and $|-5| = -(-5) = 5$. The "$-x$" does **not** mean the answer is negative: when $x$ is negative, $-x$ is positive.
Useful facts: $|x - y| = |y - x|$ (the distance between $x$ and $y$), $|xy| = |x||y|$, but $|x + y| \le |x| + |y|$ (equal only when $x, y$ have the same sign or one is 0).

cards.title: Two numbers with the same absolute value
body: 3 and $-3$ are both 3 units from 0, on opposite sides. So $|x| = 3$ has two solutions.

cards.title: 2.4.2 Absolute value equations
body: For $k > 0$: $$|u| = k \iff u = -k \text{ or } u = k$$
Solve both equations and put the answers together. Special cases: $|u| = 0$ gives only $u = 0$; $|u| = $ a negative number has **no solution** (distance cannot be negative).
Before splitting, get the absolute value **alone** on one side: $|x + 1| + 2 = 7$ → $|x + 1| = 5$ first.

cards.title: 2.4.3 Absolute value inequalities
body: For $k > 0$:
- $|u| < k \iff -k < u < k$ (distance **less** than $k$ → **between**, one piece, "and").
- $|u| > k \iff u < -k \text{ or } u > k$ (distance **more** than $k$ → **outside**, two pieces, "or").
The same holds with $\le$ and $\ge$ (then the end points are included). "And" gives the **intersection** of the two solution sets; "or" gives the **union**.

glossary.meaning: The quantity that is chosen or controlled; its values form the domain.
The quantity that depends on the independent one; its values form the range.
The set of all possible input (independent) values.
The set of all output (dependent) values.
A graph of separate points; the inputs take only separate values.
An unbroken graph; the inputs take every real value in an interval.
Equations with exactly the same solution set.
The fixed number $k$ in $y = kx$ or $xy = k$.
$|x|$, the distance of $x$ from 0 on the number line.

tips.text: Formula: |x|=a ⇒ x=±a (a≥0) Direct: double x doubles y. Inverse: double x halves y.
Count the input → discrete dots; measure it → continuous line.
Inequalities: multiply or divide by a negative → reverse the sign.
Direct: y ÷ x constant. Inverse: x × y constant.

questions.q: Inequality on a number line: closed dot means?
why: A closed (filled) dot means the end number is included, so the inequality uses ≤ or ≥. An open dot means it is excluded (< or >).
questions.label: 29. Inequality on a number line: closed dot means?

similar.a: Solve both cases and check — extras appear.

questions.answer: No solution. Case x + 1 = x is impossible; case x + 1 = −x gives x = −1/2, which fails the check.
why: Case 1: x + 1 = x gives 1 = 0, impossible. Case 2: x + 1 = −x gives x = −1/2, but then the right side x is negative while |x + 1| ≥ 0, so it fails the check. No solution. Always check absolute-value answers.

similar.q: Flip inequality when you  A) Add 3  B) Multiply by a negative  C) Add x  D) Take absolute value always

why: Answer B: Multiply by a negative
Adding or subtracting the same number keeps the order. Only multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses it (e.g. 2 < 3 but −2 > −3).
questions.tip: Read all the options before you choose; cross out the ones that belong to a different idea.

questions.q: For "the wage a person earns and the number of hours worked", name the dependent and independent quantities.
why: Step 1: say "wage depends on hours worked" — this makes sense.
Step 2: the first is dependent (wage), the second independent (hours).
questions.tip: Use the sentence "___ depends on ___".

similar.q: Area of a square and its side length?
similar.a: Area depends on the side: area dependent, side independent.
